lawyer:
Mr. BK Das, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. SK Sinha with Mr. Mahbub Ali, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Idris Mia (Md.) ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Promode Ranjan Das & others ----- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
K. M. Hasan, J.: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause why the order passed on 26.10.79 by the Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, in Misc. Appeal No. 181 of 1977, affirming the order dated 18.3.77 of the Munsif, Second Court. Sylhet in Misc. Case No. 148 of 73 allowing an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, should not be set aside. 

 2. The pre-emptor, Promode Ranjan Das, filed Misc. Case No. 148 of 1973 in the second Court of Munsif, Moulvibazar under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the pre-emptee purchaser and petitioner in this revision petition and other opposite parties alleging, inter alia that the case land belonged to opposite parties 4 and 5, who sold the same to the opposite parties 1-3 by a kabala dated 27.4.73. The pre-emptor claims that though he is a contiguous land holder he did not know about the transfer but he came to know about it in the month to Sravan, 1380 BS. On coming to know about it he took the certified copy of the kabala on 17.8.73 and filed the above mentioned Misc. Case No. 148/73 on 11.9.73 on proper deposit of consideration and compensation. He further claims that the purchasers are strangers to the case land and as such the land is liable to be pre-empted. 

 10. Mr. BK Das, the learned Advocate submits that the purchaser pre-emptee, who is also the petitioner in the revision petition, is not required to file an application for proportional pre-emption under section 96(5)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1951 as the purchaser pre-emptee is not a stranger to the case land but a person holding land contiguous to the case land. He further argues that it is particularly not necessary as the purchaser pre-emptee has already been resisting a pre-emption application. He submits that the purpose of section 96 of the said Act is to disallow strangers from holding land, but the pre-emptee is not stranger rather he is an admitted contiguous landowner. Therefore, courts below have erred in law in insisting on an application from him for proportionate pre-emption. I find it difficult to accept this argument as section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quite clear that intending pre-emptee, whether co-sharers by inheritance, co-sharer by purchase or a holder of contiguous land shall have to file a pre-emption application within a specific period of time. By not doing so the pre-emptee, Idris Mia, had simply waived his right to pre-empt the case land. 

 11. At the time of the hearing of this revision petition the learned advocate for the pre-emptee purchaser, the petitioner in the revision petition, took for the first time a ground that the pre-emption application is not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said section read with section 90 of the said Act requires a specific averment in the application for pre-emption that the pre-emptor is a bonafide cultivator. But there is no such averment in the application for pre-emption. He further submits that while granting pre-emption the Court is required to give finding that the pre-emptor does not hold more than 60 bighas of land and that he is a bonafide cultivator. In support he cites a single bench decision held in Nayeb Ali and others Vs. Akhtar Rahman and others 29 DLR 153 in which it is held "in the absence of a finding that a pre-emptor "is a person to whom transfer of the holding or a portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under section 96 the application for pre-emption is bound to fail." 

 12. A close scrutiny of the application for pre-emption will show that though in the body there is no specific averment that the pre-emptor is a bonafide cultivator but in its cause title the profession of the pre-emptor is clearly stated as "গৃহস্থী" the dictionary meaning of which is a "house holder" but in the context of the village life in Bangladesh and in a wider sense it includes a cultivator also. If the purchaser pre-emptee intended to dispute that the pre-emptor is a bonafide cultivator he should have specifically and sufficiently denied in his written statement that the pre-emptor is not a bonafide cultivator but a mere "গৃহস্থী" or a house holder. 

 "Every allegation of fact in the plaint if not denied specifically or by necessary implication or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability". 

 14. This rule is known as the doctrine of non-traverse which means that when a material averment is passed over by an evasive denial or without a specific denial it is taken to be admitted. Here in this case there is no denial by the pre-emptee that the pre-emptor is a bonafide cultivator. Mr. Das argues that there cannot be any denial as there is no specific averment in the pre-emption application. He argues that Order 7(1)(e) of the Civil Procedure Code requires that an application should contain the facts which constitute the cause of action so that there can be specific denial in the written statement under Order  rule 3 and issues can be framed under Order 14 of the Civil Procedure Code. 

 15. In view of the fact that the pre-emptor has clearly stated, in the cause title of his application for pre-emption, that he is a "গৃহস্থী" I do not find any non-fulfillment of the above mentioned legal requirements under the Civil Procedure Code by the pre-emptor. By stating in the cause title his profession as "গৃহস্থী" he has made it obligatory for the pre-emptee to specifically deny in his written statement that the pre-emptor is not a bonafide cultivator. The cause title very much forms a part of the application, and statement made therein should be denied specifically or by implication. 

 16. Lastly, if the submission of Mr. Das is accepted i.e. there is no averment in the body of the application for pre-emption and what is stated in the cause title is not an averment and as a result the pre-emption application should fail, even then the revisional application is liable to be rejected because of the decision in the case of Matiur Rahman Vs. Md. Iman Ali @ Md. Iman Miah and others 1981 BLD (AD) 280 wherein it has been held, that mere omission to make an assertion in respect of ceiling of land in the application by the pre-emptors or to adduce evidence to this effect in the absence of any averment to the contrary, will not render the application liable to be dismissed and an omission to record a finding to this affect in such a circumstance cannot be a ground for dismissal of the pre-emption case. 

 17. In the written statement filed before the trial Court and in the appeal before the lower Appellate Court no specific allegation has been made by the pre-emptee purchaser that the pre-emptor has omitted to make an averment as required by section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that, the pre-emptor is a bonafide cultivator. This ground has been taken for the first time at the time of the hearing of the revisional petition, whereas this objection should have been taken at the earliest possible opportunity. For failure to do so, the pre-emptee purchaser may be deemed to have waived his right to object the pre-emption application. Similar view has been held in the case of Akhtarunnessa and others Vs. Habibullah & others 31 DLR (AD) 88 regarding the omission of a necessary party.
